Provides working code for a faithfulness/groundedness check (decompose answer into atomic claims, verify each against retrieved context) and a DeepEval pytest CI gate using G-Eval with a custom plain-language rubric and pass/fail threshold (e.g. 0.7) that blocks merge on regression. Documents three published LLM-judge biases with primary citations: (1) position bias -- an IJCNLP 2025 systematic study evaluated 15 LLM judges across ~150,000 evaluation instances and found judges systematically favor whichever response sits in a particular prompt slot, independent of content, with verdicts flipping purely from reordering; (2) self-preference bias -- models disproportionately favor outputs from themselves or their own model family, inflating scores when e.g. GPT-4o judges GPT-4o's own output; (3) verbosity bias -- longer responses are rated higher regardless of whether the added length adds useful content. Flags the commonly cited '~80% LLM-judge/human agreement' statistic (from the original MT-Bench paper) as an aggregate benchmark figure, not a production-readiness guarantee for a specific task/judge-model combination. Provides a complete position-bias detection harness: run the same pairwise comparison twice with response order swapped, measure the verdict-flip ('inconsistency') rate, and treat scores with skepticism if that rate is meaningfully above 0%; mitigation is averaging scores across both orderings or using a judge model from a different model family than the one being evaluated.

data.title: Large Language Model based Multi-Agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges
data.summary:
IJCAI 2024 survey (arXiv:2402.01680; Guo, Chen, Wang, Chang, Pei, Chawla, Wiest, Zhang — Notre Dame/KAUST/SUSTech/UMass Boston) of LLM-based multi-agent systems, organized around agent profiling, communication, and capability-acquisition mechanisms, with a comparative taxonomy table spanning Problem Solving (software development, embodied agents, science experiments/debate) and World Simulation (society, policy, economy) applications.

Software-development subsection frames multi-agent code generation as role emulation following waterfall-style processes: each cited system (Qian et al. 2023/ChatDev, Hong et al. 2023/MetaGPT, Dong et al. 2023b) assigns pre-defined or model-generated role profiles (CTO/programmer, Product Manager/Engineer, Analyst/coder), uses a sandboxed agent-environment interface, cooperative interaction paradigm, and layered structure (MetaGPT additionally uses a 'Shared Message Pool' for cross-agent communication). All three systems draw capability growth from the same three sources: environment feedback, agent-interaction feedback, and human feedback, adjusted via memory mechanisms and self-evolution.

The taxonomy table's columns (motivation/domain, agent-environment interface, profiling method, example profiles, interaction paradigm — cooperative vs. debate, structure — centralized/decentralized/layered, feedback source, adjustment mechanism) function as a reusable framework for classifying any new multi-agent software-factory design against the literature: e.g. debate-based systems (Du et al. 2023 'Improving Factuality', Xiong et al. 2023 inter-consistency examination, Chan et al. 2023 ChatEval) use decentralized/centralized structure with proponent-opponent-judge profiles and no sandbox, contrasting with cooperative software-dev systems' sandboxed, layered design. Useful as the architectural vocabulary underlying the whitepaper's Advanced Skill Sequences and Multi-Agent Orchestration pillars; the companion GitHub repo (taichengguo/LLM_MultiAgents_Survey_Papers) extends this bibliography with entries through 2026.

data.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge
data.summary: Primary paper (Zheng, Chiang, Sheng et al. — UC Berkeley, UCSD, CMU, Stanford, MBZUAI; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks track; 13,647 words — LONG, flagged for source-analyst delegation) establishing LLM-as-a-judge as a scalable evaluation method and introducing MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Verified numeric claim: strong LLM judges like GPT-4 achieve OVER 80% agreement with both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences — described as 'the same level of agreement between humans' — this is the exact primary-source number that Confident AI's secondary blog post rounds to '85% vs 81%.' The paper explicitly names and examines three LLM-judge bias/limitation categories: position bias (preferring the first-shown answer in pairwise comparison), verbosity bias (preferring longer responses regardless of quality), and self-enhancement bias (a model favoring outputs from its own model family), plus limited reasoning ability as a general limitation, and proposes mitigations for each. Demonstrates MT-bench (multi-turn question set) and Chatbot Arena (crowdsourced pairwise battle platform) as public benchmarks (3K expert votes, 30K human-preference conversations, released via github.com/lm-sys/FastChat) that make LLM-judge/human-agreement verification reproducible. Also shows MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena benchmarks complement traditional multiple-choice benchmarks (MMLU, HELM) by capturing instruction-following/alignment quality that those benchmarks cannot distinguish between base and RLHF-aligned models. This is the foundational primary source for essentially every 'LLM-as-judge aligns with humans at X%' claim circulating in 2026 vendor content (Confident AI, DeepEval) — cite this paper's 80%+ figure as the verified original number rather than secondary paraphrases.

data.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? - Model Context Protocol
data.summary: Official MCP (Model Context Protocol) docs intro page. MCP is an open-source standard, analogized to 'a USB-C port for AI applications,' for connecting AI applications/agents to external data sources (local files, databases), tools (search engines, calculators), and workflows (specialized prompts). data.title: GitHub - addyosmani/agent-skills: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents. · GitHub
data.summary:
Root repo for addyosmani/agent-skills (105.2k stars, 11.0k forks, 528 watchers as fetched — a very widely adopted open-source library), 'Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents,' created by Addy Osmani (Google Chrome engineering lead) with collaborators Federico Bartoli and Joan Leon. Directly operationalizes the 'SOPs to Agent Skills' pillar at scale: packages 25 skills (24 lifecycle skills + 1 meta-skill 'using-agent-skills') mapped to a DEFINE->PLAN->BUILD->VERIFY->REVIEW->SHIP lifecycle, each exposed as a slash command (/spec, /plan, /build, /test, /constraints, /review, /webperf, /code-simplify, /ship) that auto-activates the relevant skill. Notably offers '/build auto': approve a plan once, then the agent implements every task in a single autonomous pass while still requiring per-task tests and commits and pausing on failures/risky steps — a concrete named pattern for 'self-sustaining agentic loops' with bounded autonomy (directly relevant to the Continuous Operation pillar).

Every skill follows a fixed anatomy: Frontmatter (name/description) -> Overview -> When to Use -> Process (step-by-step workflow) -> Rationalizations (documented agent excuses + rebuttals for skipping steps) -> Red Flags -> Verification (evidence requirements: tests passing, build output, runtime data — 'Seems right is never sufficient'). This 'Anti-rationalization' table pattern and mandatory Verification section is a reusable template for encoding rigid evals directly into Agent Skills across any domain, not just performance (as seen in the sibling performance-optimization skill). Notable individual skills map directly onto the whitepaper's pillars: 'doubt-driven-development' implements an adversarial CLAIM->EXTRACT->DOUBT->RECONCILE->STOP review loop with optional user-authorized cross-model escalation for high-stakes changes — essentially a formalized adversarial-model-review protocol; 'source-driven-development' grounds every framework decision in official docs with citation and explicit flagging of unverified claims (zero-hallucination pillar); 'context-engineering' addresses rules files/context packing/MCP integration (context isolation pillar); 'security-and-hardening' covers OWASP Top 10, secrets management, dependency auditing; 'constraint-driven-development' interviews for a quality bar and explicitly catches 'agents silencing checks or skipping tests to get green' — a direct anti-gaming-of-evals mechanism. Also ships 4 pre-configured specialist agent personas (code-reviewer, test-engineer, security-auditor, web-performance-auditor) with an explicit 'personas don't invoke personas' orchestration rule documented in references/orchestration-patterns.md. Distribution covers 70+ agent hosts (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, OpenCode, Antigravity, Kiro) via an installer CLI ('npx skills add'), illustrating the real-world cross-surface packaging/distribution challenge for Agent Skills noted elsewhere (e.g. Anthropic's own docs state custom Skills don't sync across surfaces). MIT licensed.

data.title: RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy
data.summary: Primary RAGTruth paper (Niu, Wu, Zhu et al. — NewsBreak, UIUC; 7,950 words). Introduces RAGTruth, a corpus of nearly 18,000 naturally generated LLM responses under standard RAG setups, manually annotated at both the case level and the word/span level for hallucination type and intensity (e.g., 'Evident Conflict' spans where the generation directly contradicts the retrieved passage, illustrated with a worked ultrasound-timing example). Benchmarks hallucination frequency across different LLMs under RAG and critically evaluates existing hallucination-detection methods against this ground truth. Key finding: fine-tuning a relatively small LLM on RAGTruth achieves hallucination-detection performance competitive with prompt-based detection using state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4, and the fine-tuned detector can be used to actively mitigate hallucination in downstream LLM responses — i.e., a purpose-built small detector can match GPT-4-as-judge detection accuracy at presumably lower cost/latency, directly relevant to the query's cost-optimization pillar for an eval/guardrail layer. This is the dataset-level primary source behind the Future AGI blog's RAG-citation-contract hallucination-reduction claim; it establishes RAG-under-hallucination measurement methodology (span-level annotation) rather than being the source of the specific '50%+ reduction' percentage cited secondhand.

data.title: Efficient Serving for Dynamic Agent Workflows with Prediction-based KV-Cache Management
data.summary: ArXiv paper (Zheng, Fu, Wu, Yuan, Zhang, Wang, Zhu, Yan, Jiang; Wuhan University + SJTU + Macquarie + HKUST + Dameng Database, May 2026, cs.LG) introduces PBKV (Prediction-Based KV-Cache Management), a serving-layer system for multi-agent LLM workflows (e.g., LangChain/AutoGen/MetaGPT Planner-Coder-Tester pipelines) that predicts future agent invocations several steps ahead from historical workflow traces plus the current task's context, then uses that probabilistic forecast to decide which KV-cache entries to keep in GPU memory versus evict/prefetch. Problem framing: KV-cache reuse across agents in a workflow can exceed 90% hit rate in principle, but GPU memory is limited and standard LRU eviction is misaligned with workflow structure (cache can sit idle through tool calls/agent transitions before being reused, so LRU evicts it prematurely); the existing SOTA, KVFlow, fixes this only by assuming a static, predefined agent invocation DAG, which breaks on realistic dynamic workflows (e.g., a Tester sending code back for rewriting, a Retriever spawning new sub-queries). PBKV's predictor (~350K parameters, processes a batch of 1,024 requests in 1.56ms) fuses cross-workflow historical transition patterns with per-request semantic signals and forecasts K future agent-invocation steps; on the HoVer+LangChain workload it reaches 0.94 next-agent-prediction accuracy at 1-step horizon and 0.77 at 3-step horizon (trained on 1K traces, tested on 500). Two robustness mechanisms guard against prediction error: (1) hierarchical/lifecycle-aware eviction that reclaims 'retired' cache from terminated workflows first (a simple deterministic rule that alone improves average hit rate up to 1.66x), then ranks remaining active cache by a predictor-driven lookahead reuse score; (2) conservative prefetching that only consumes otherwise-idle GPU memory/PCIe bandwidth so mispredictions cannot regress performance below baseline (an ablation shows aggressive prefetching only marginally beats conservative prefetching when noise is below 20%, and degrades below the conservative baseline as prediction noise/budget grows, confirming conservative prefetching is the safer default under the admittedly hard-to-predict agentic workloads). Evaluated on three workflow benchmarks across two LLMs (Qwen3-14B/32B) against LRU and KVFlow: PBKV achieves up to 1.85x speedup over LRU on dynamic workflows and up to 1.26x speedup over KVFlow on static workflows; on the HoVer+LangChain/Qwen3-14B workload at concurrency 72, LRU's steady-state cache hit rate collapses to below 30% (around 10% under sustained pressure) while PBKV's lifecycle-aware variant reaches 66.01% and the full PBKV (with speculative prefetching) reaches 69.10%. Ablations show prediction accuracy monotonically determines downstream hit-rate gains across predictor backbones (MLP, GCN, Markov, kNN, linear baselines all tested), and the learned transformer-based predictor outperforms every baseline family at every lookahead horizon, with Markov baselines saturating early while the learned predictor continues to scale with more training data.

data.title: FACTSCORE: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of
data.summary: Primary FActScore paper (Min, Krishna, Lyu et al. — U Washington, UMass Amherst, AI2, Meta AI; 15,305 words — LONG, flagged for source-analyst delegation). Introduces FACTSCORE: decompose a long-form LLM generation into atomic facts, then compute the percentage supported by a reliable knowledge source — explicitly solving the problem that binary factual/non-factual judgments are inadequate because a single generation mixes supported and unsupported claims. Concrete measured numbers: human-evaluated FActScore of ChatGPT-generated biographies is only 58%; an automated FActScore estimator using retrieval plus a strong LLM judge achieves under 2% error rate vs. human evaluation; applying the automated metric to 6,500 generations from 13 recent LMs would have cost 6,000 if done by human annotators. Findings: GPT-4 and ChatGPT are measurably more factual than public/open models; Vicuna and Alpaca rank among the best public models by this metric. This is the primary benchmark underlying the Future AGI blog's claim that 'a tight RAG pipeline cuts unsupported claims by half or more compared to a closed book baseline' — the FActScore paper itself establishes the atomic-fact-decomposition methodology rather than directly measuring the RAG-vs-closed-book delta cited secondhand; treat that specific percentage as the secondary source's interpretation, not a number stated verbatim in this paper's abstract.

data.title: OpenAI Agents SDK vs LangGraph vs Autogen vs CrewAI | Composio
data.summary: Composio hands-on comparison of OpenAI Agents SDK vs LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen, with a working code walkthrough (OpenAI Agents SDK + Composio toolset building a GitHub-starring agent via function_tool and Runner.run). OpenAI Agents SDK's three core primitives: Agents (LLM + instructions + tools), Handoffs (delegate to another agent), Guardrails (parallel input/output validation that can abort execution early -- directly relevant to Pillar 1 rigid evals). Comparison table findings: OpenAI Agents SDK has the lowest learning curve and built-in tracing/visualization for debugging but 'limited built-in support' for parallel execution and lower production-readiness maturity (framework is new); LangGraph has the steepest learning curve but the most sophisticated state management (graph edges, conditional transitions, LangSmith integration) and is explicitly rated 'highly scalable' and production-ready, best for complex cyclical workflows; CrewAI offers the most intuitive role-based mental model and built-in short/long-term/entity/user memory, rated production-ready for crew-based workflows; AutoGen (Microsoft-backed) excels at flexible conversation topologies and agent networks but has 'limited' human-in-the-loop support (only never/always/at-termination) and no built-in time-travel debugging. Notes OpenAI Agents SDK is distinct from OpenAI's earlier Swarm framework. Author's recommendation: OpenAI Agents SDK for simplicity+production with tight OpenAI integration; LangGraph for complex/cyclical multi-agent production systems; CrewAI for intuitive role-based teams; AutoGen for research-grade flexible conversation patterns.

data.title: Reducing Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Code
data.summary:
ACM paper (Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol 10, No. OOPSLA2, Article 393/111, Oct 2026; arXiv:2511.12288; authors Dai, Liang, Xu, Xie, Mechtaev — Peking University) introduces 'semantic triangulation,' a theory-grounded framework for reducing LLM code hallucinations at selection time (post-generation, black-box). Problem framing: standard plurality voting over multiple LLM-generated code samples fails because LLMs produce correlated errors — sampled programs can 'collude' on the same wrong answer, so voting amplifies shared mistakes rather than catching them. Existing proxy-based approaches (LLM-generated tests, auto-formalized specifications) suffer the same flaw since the proxies come from the same imperfect model that wrote the code.

Core mechanism: transform the original problem into a 'dissociative variant' likely requiring a fundamentally different algorithm (via problem inversion, decomposition, or solution enumeration — 4 concrete triangulation methods instantiated), then check consistency between independently sampled solutions to the original and the transformed problem. The paper proves, under a formal model of LLM hallucination, that this decorrelation property confers higher confidence in program correctness than correlated-error methods.

Empirical results (LiveCodeBench and CodeElo benchmarks, across GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash): the method increases the probability of selecting a correct program by 16% over baselines (test generation, metamorphic testing, auto-formalized specifications), and achieves 7% higher reliability and 7% higher F1 score in selection-or-abstention scenarios. It is reported as the only evaluated method that consistently handles 'inexact' problems admitting multiple valid solutions — a known failure mode for exact-match and test-based proxies. Directly load-bearing for the whitepaper's Zero-Hallucination / Rigid Evals pillar: provides a concrete, provable mechanism for decorrelating LLM self-verification signals rather than relying on majority vote or same-model-generated tests, which is exactly the trap naive LLM-as-judge adversarial review setups can fall into.

data.title: Towards Autonomous Software Development
data.summary: Full position paper (22,104 words — LONG, flagged for source-analyst delegation) behind the Berkeley RDI blog post, authored by Hao Wang, Ion Stoica, Dawn Song (UC Berkeley), with CISPA, MIT, Cursor, UT Austin, UC Irvine, Microsoft co-authors. Core argument: the research community should study software development as 'a trajectory of substitutions for increasing autonomy, where responsibilities, risks, and failure modes fundamentally shift,' rather than as isolated task-level AI-assistance improvements. Decomposes the SDLC into requirement curation, system design, implementation, testing, and deployment, then defines the three-level autonomy taxonomy (Code/Pipeline/Demand Autonomy) modeled explicitly on SAE autonomous-driving levels. Names 'intent preservation' as the unifying research problem across all three levels — as direct human control recedes, the challenge is ensuring the AI system faithfully executes what the human actually wanted, not just what was literally specified. Organizes a research agenda around five areas: specification understanding, security/verification, system-level concerns (agent-centric language/infrastructure design), human-agent interaction, and economic modeling of hybrid development. States explicitly the paper does not advocate for unbounded or accelerated autonomy, but seeks a conceptual framework making responsibility/risk/control shifts explicit as autonomy increases. This is the primary source underlying essentially all of the Berkeley blog's structural-shift and ten-predictions claims; cite this directly rather than the blog summary where exact wording matters.

data.title: AI Agent Development Costs: Why Sandbox Billing Breaks | Blaxel
data.summary: Blaxel (agent sandbox vendor) blog post arguing traditional per-hour/per-token sandbox billing structurally mismatches how coding agents actually consume compute, with Blaxel's own GB-second/standby billing presented as the fix (vendor content -- treat product claims skeptically, but the underlying benchmark citations are useful). Key cited numbers: agentic workflows consume 20-30x more tokens per interaction than standard chat; API calls per coding task range from 35.5 to 181 depending on architecture (SWE-bench benchmark: one config averaged 35.5 API calls / 440,000 input tokens, another used 181 calls / 8.1M input tokens with worse outcomes); per-task costs range /usr/bin/bash.10-.00 at similar accuracy, with 13x-32x cost gaps between best/worst model combos at matched accuracy; input context grows 3-4x per iteration loop. On idle-compute waste specifically (directly relevant to auto-killing idle agents): a cited GPU energy study found online-serving workloads spend 61% of in-execution time in an execution-idle state, consuming 48% of energy during those idle intervals; real-world infrastructure audits show average utilization below 20%; GCP Cloud Run enforces a 1-minute minimum billing period per instance and Azure Functions Flex Consumption charges for always-ready idle instances; container restart/re-initialization overhead consumes 31-48% of total task time when state isn't persisted (e.g. git clone of an 8.9GB repo takes over 6 minutes). Blaxel's countermeasure: sandboxes transition to a zero-compute-cost standby state after 15 seconds of network inactivity (only storage/snapshot charges continue) and resume from standby in under 25ms with full state restored via microVM isolation -- i.e., aggressive idle-triggered suspension rather than full agent self-termination, preserving state for instant resume. Also cites AWS research showing a 37% performance gap between lab and production conditions for agentic systems, inflating effective per-task cost from failures.

data.title: Knowledge Graph for Code Explained: A Practical Guide
data.summary: Pharaoh (vendor) blog explaining code knowledge graphs as a structural-intelligence layer for AI coding agents: nodes are code entities (functions, files, modules, endpoints, cron handlers, env vars), edges are relationships (calls, imports, exports, depends-on, reachable-from), contrasted with grep (text match), AST (syntax only), and vector search (similarity only) which cannot answer relationship questions like blast radius or production reachability. Pharaoh's own implementation parses TypeScript/Python repos with Tree-sitter (deterministic parsing, not LLM-guessed), stores relationships in Neo4j, and exposes queryable tools (codebase mapping, function search/dedup, blast-radius analysis, dead-code detection, reachability checking, dependency tracing, cross-repo auditing) to agents via MCP. Claims graph queries return the same architectural answer a file-reading agent would need ~40K tokens for in roughly 2K tokens, with zero further LLM cost per query after initial mapping (map once, query deterministically many times). Gives a worked example: refactoring a shared  function without graph context missed two transitive callers reachable from  and a cron job, producing a silent regression; with blast-radius output the risk and downstream impact are surfaced before the edit. Recommends adopting the pattern only when codebase is an active product with daily AI-agent use, growing module sprawl, and real refactor regression risk — not for small/throwaway repos.

data.title: Claude Agents | Anthropic Agent SDK Consulting | OneWave AI
data.summary: OneWave AI (Anthropic consulting partner) marketing/overview page distinguishing Anthropic's two agent-building paths relevant to Pillar 5 architecture decisions: (1) Managed Agents -- Anthropic's hosted autonomous agent runtime launched April 2026, where Anthropic handles infrastructure, scaling, monitoring, and safety controls; fastest path to production (1-2 weeks), lower engineering overhead, but less control, best for standard workflows; (2) Agent SDK -- released April 2025, developer toolkit exposing agent loops, tool definitions, context management, multi-agent handoffs, and guardrails as primitives for self-hosted agents; full control over orchestration/data residency but full operational responsibility, 3-5 weeks for a multi-agent system with MCP integrations and full monitoring. States most production deployments combine both: managed agents for standard workflows, SDK for specialized/proprietary orchestration. Lists required production controls mirroring Pillar 1/5 concerns: structured logging of every action/decision, human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes operations, hard per-run cost/budget limits, output validation against quality criteria, escalation rules, real-time oversight dashboards, retry logic, state persistence, error recovery, graceful degradation. Vendor content with sales intent; treat specific dates/timelines as vendor claims rather than verified facts.

data.title: GitHub - janus-llm/janus-llm: Leveraging LLMs for modernization through intelligent chunking, iterative prompting and reflection, and retrieval augmented generation (RAG). · GitHub
data.summary: Open-source MITRE Corporation tool (janus-llm, Apache-2.0 license, 42 stars/7 forks as fetched) for LLM-assisted legacy IT modernization, used in the MITRE arXiv:2411.14971 study. Directly relevant to the Reverse Engineering & Codebase Mastery pillar: capabilities include chunking code in 100+ programming languages into a Chroma vector database sized to fit model context windows, file-by-file LLM-driven source-to-source translation between languages, and BINARY-TO-SOURCE translation via Ghidra decompilation integration — a concrete real tool combining neural decompilation with LLM reasoning. Also generates requirements, UML diagrams, code comments, and summaries from source code, plus built-in evaluation of generated artifacts, exposed via a CLI tool ('janus'). Tech stack: Python, LangChain, ChromaDB, tree-sitter (for code parsing/chunking). This is a usable, installable (pip install janus-llm) building block for a reverse-engineering/legacy-codebase-ingestion pipeline in the software-factory architecture, not just a research prototype description.

data.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents \ Anthropic
data.summary: Primary Anthropic engineering post (published Jan 9, 2026; authored by Mikaela Grace, Jeremy Hadfield, Rodrigo Olivares, Jiri De Jonghe) setting out Anthropic's internal methodology for evaluating AI agents, drawn from building Claude Code and collaborating with customers (iGent, Cognition, Bolt, Sierra, Vals.ai, Macroscope, PromptLayer, Stripe, Shopify). Defines core vocabulary: task/trial/grader/transcript/outcome/evaluation harness/agent harness/evaluation suite. Describes three grader types — code-based (fast, cheap, objective, but brittle to valid variation), model-based (flexible, scalable, handles nuance, but non-deterministic and needs human calibration), and human (gold-standard but slow/expensive) — and recommends combining them with weighted/binary/hybrid scoring. Distinguishes capability evals (start at low pass rate, target weaknesses) from regression evals (should stay near 100%, catch backsliding); capability evals 'graduate' into regression suites once saturated. Covers agent-type-specific eval design: coding agents (SWE-bench Verified rose 40%->80%+ in a year; Terminal-Bench for end-to-end tasks), conversational agents (τ-Bench/τ2-Bench with LLM-simulated users), research agents (BrowseComp; groundedness/coverage/source-quality graders), computer-use agents (WebArena, OSWorld; DOM vs. screenshot tradeoffs). Introduces pass@k (chance of >=1 success in k trials) vs pass^k (chance all k succeed) as complementary non-determinism metrics that diverge sharply as k grows. Gives an explicit eval-building roadmap (8 steps: start with 20-50 real-failure tasks, write unambiguous tasks with reference solutions, build balanced problem sets, build isolated stable harnesses, design graders resistant to gaming, read transcripts, watch for eval saturation, maintain suites with dedicated eval-infra teams plus domain-expert task contribution). Cites concrete failure cases: Opus 4.5 initially scored only 42% on CORE-Bench due to grading bugs (rigid numeric matching, ambiguous specs, stochastic tasks) before jumping to 95% after fixes; METR found misconfigured time-horizon benchmark tasks that penalized models for following instructions. Appendix surveys eval frameworks: Harbor (containerized trials, Terminal-Bench 2.0 registry), Braintrust (offline eval + production observability, autoevals library), LangSmith, Langfuse (self-hosted), Arize Phoenix/AX.

data.title: Practical Loop Engineering - by Addy Osmani - Elevate
data.summary: Addy Osmani (Chrome/Google engineering leader turned independent writer) practitioner account of 'loop engineering' in Claude Code/Codex, directly load-bearing for Pillar 5 (triggers, continuous operation) and Pillar 2 (SOPs/Agent Skills/probabilistic sequences). Describes running 5-10 agents in parallel daily, maxing concurrently at ~5. Defines a loop as 'an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met.' Documents the Claude Code team's four-tier loop taxonomy: (1) manual/agentic loop -- single-turn, human directs each turn; (2) goal-based loop via /goal primitive -- an independent evaluator model checks a user-defined deterministic stopping condition (e.g. 'Lighthouse score >= 92, stop after 10 turns') each time Claude tries to stop, preventing the agent from self-judging 'good enough'; (3) time-based loop via /loop (runs on a fixed interval, e.g. every 1h/24h, session-scoped, expires 7 days after creation, stops when session ends unless resumed with --resume/--continue); (4) proactive/scheduled loops via /schedule, which move execution to the cloud with no human in real time, triggered by event/schedule, routing routine work to smaller/faster models and reserving capable models for judgment calls. Gives verbatim example prompts: '/goal Refactor the data-fetching layer in Dashboard.tsx until Lighthouse performance score is >= 92 and LCP is under 1.8s... Do not change the public API of any hooks. Abort if two consecutive turns show no improvement. Stop after 10 turns.' and a verify-frontend-change Agent Skill requiring the agent to start a dev server, interact with the UI, screenshot before/after, check the browser console for zero new errors, and run a Lighthouse/Core Web Vitals audit before declaring any UI change complete -- a concrete rigid-eval pattern for Pillar 1. Describes a dual-agent verification discipline: 'the other habit that matters here is not letting the agent that did the work decide the work is good. One sub-agent drafts the change. A separate one verifies it' -- directly supports adversarial model review (Pillar 1). Documents a real production workflow: an 80K-star open-source repo receiving 80-90 PRs/day, now triaged via /loop every 1h checking GitHub issues/PRs against contribution guidelines, combined with /goal for implementation. Flags failure modes: loops are a poor fit for vague/subjective goals ('keep going until this UI design is good'); a classic stuck-loop signal is the same command retried 3x with no change in result; the /goal evaluator only checks whether hard rules were met against the transcript, it does not judge quality -- judgment must stay with the human or a separate verifying agent.

data.title: CyberGym: Evaluating AI Agents' Real-World Cybersecurity Capabilities at Scale
data.summary:
CyberGym (Wang, Shi, He, Cai, Zhang, Song — ICLR 2026, openreview id 2YvbLQEdYt) is a benchmark of 1,507 real-world vulnerability-reproduction instances collected from OSS-Fuzz across 188 large software projects. Level-1 task: given a vulnerability description and the unpatched codebase (often spanning thousands of files / millions of LOC), the agent must generate a proof-of-concept that triggers on the pre-patch version but not the post-patch version. Beyond static benchmarking, open-ended discovery runs (OpenHands + GPT-4.1 / GPT-5 across 431 OSS-Fuzz projects, 1,748 executables) found: GPT-4.1 triggered 16 crashes -> 7 confirmed zero-days; GPT-5 triggered 56 crashes -> 22 confirmed zero-days (4 overlapping). Across the full evaluation, agent-generated PoCs surfaced 34 zero-day vulnerabilities and 18 historically incomplete patches total (17 confirmed incomplete patches across 15 projects from 759 crash-triggering PoCs across 60 projects); zero-days persisted an average of 969 days before discovery.

Key capability findings with exact numbers: (1) thinking/extended-reasoning mode raises GPT-5's success rate from 7.7% (minimal reasoning) to 22.0% (high reasoning) on a 300-task subset, surpassing Claude-Sonnet-4; (2) richer input context matters heavily — only 3.5% of instances are reproducible at level 0 (text description only, no stack trace/patch); (3) PoC length is a major difficulty driver — agents achieve highest success on PoCs under 10 bytes but drop to ~10% success on PoCs over 100 bytes, which make up 65.7% of the benchmark; (4) with OpenHands/Claude-4-Sonnet and a 100-step cap, successful runs concentrate in steps 20-80 (peak 20-50) and nearly half of all runs terminate at 80-100 steps without success, suggesting a 100-step budget is a reasonable solve/resource tradeoff. This is the strongest available empirical anchor in this batch for the '90-minute cyber-security sweep' pillar — it demonstrates current frontier-model ceiling and failure modes on autonomous vulnerability discovery/reproduction at realistic codebase scale, with load-bearing, non-rounded statistics throughout.

data.title: Adaptive heterogeneous multi-agent debate for enhanced educational and factual reasoning in large language models | Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences | Springer Nature Link
data.summary: Peer-reviewed open-access paper (Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences, Springer, published 24 Nov 2025, vol. 37 article 330; 13,880 words -- flag for source-analyst deep-dive) proposing Adaptive Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (A-HMAD), directly load-bearing for pillar 1 (adversarial model review / zero-hallucination QC). Extends Du et al. (2023)'s homogeneous multi-agent debate baseline with three innovations: (i) diverse specialized agent roles (named 'Solver', 'Checker', 'Knowledge Guru' for factual recall, plus a strategic-planning role), (ii) a dynamic coordination policy that selects which agents contribute each round based on question domain and evolving debate state, (iii) a learned consensus optimizer f_phi that weights each agent's vote by reliability and argument confidence rather than simple majority vote. Evaluated on six benchmarks (arithmetic QA, GSM8K, MMLU, factual biography generation, chess strategy, plus TruthfulQA as a side experiment) against single-model baselines and the original homogeneous-debate method. Headline results: 4-6% absolute accuracy gains over standard homogeneous debate; >30% reduction in factual errors on biography-fact generation; heterogeneous debate beats homogeneous debate by +5.7% on arithmetic, +6.2% on GSM8K, +5.4% on MMLU. Learned-consensus ablation on 50 GSM8K disagreement cases: majority vote scored 68% correct (34/50) vs. learned consensus 78% correct (39/50), a 31% relative error reduction; using majority vote instead of learned consensus for A-HMAD's final answers would drop GSM8K accuracy from 90.2% to ~88.5% and MMLU from 76.5% to ~74.7% (1.5-2% of total system gains attributable to consensus weighting alone). Role-ablation sensitivity analysis: removing the Knowledge Guru role dropped accuracy 2.3-2.8% on GSM8K/MMLU; merging Solver+Checker into one hybrid role dropped accuracy 3.5-4.1%; duplicating a role (two Checkers) yielded <0.5% gain, showing role diversity matters more than agent count. Scaling study: accuracy on Arithmetic rises 72% (1 agent) to 87% (3) to 90% (5) to 91% (7 agents) -- diminishing returns past 5 agents; on MMLU 64%/76%/78%/78.5% for N=1/3/5/7. Debate-round scaling on Arithmetic: 0 rounds (initial-answer majority) 75%, 1 round 83%, 2 rounds 87.5%, 3 rounds 89% -- two rounds captured most of the gain. On TruthfulQA, adding a skepticism-specialized agent reduced false answers by ~20% versus a single LLM. Agent convergence (unanimous agreement) reached 92% on arithmetic and 85% on GSM8K under A-HMAD, versus 88%/80% for the homogeneous baseline -- heterogeneity increased rather than decreased convergence. Includes a worked case study showing a Checker agent catching a Solver's arithmetic mistake and a Knowledge Guru correcting a fabricated PhD-year guess (1980 guessed vs. 1978 actual) that both Solver and Checker had expressed uncertainty about -- directly illustrative of adversarial cross-checking mechanics applicable to a software factory's code-review agent roles.

data.title: Act While Thinking: Accelerating LLM Agents via Pattern-Aware Speculative Tool Execution
data.summary: ArXiv paper (Sui, Zhao, Ma, He, Wang, Li, Yang; SJTU + Microsoft Research + Stevens Institute, March 2026, cs.DC) introduces PASTE (Pattern-Aware Speculative Tool Execution), a serving-layer system that mines a developer/agent's historical tool-call traces to probabilistically predict and pre-execute the next tool call(s) before the LLM finishes 'thinking,' hiding tool latency behind LLM generation. Motivation: across Deep Research Bench, SWE-bench, and ScholarQA benchmarks, tool execution (not LLM generation) is the dominant latency cost — 60% of latency in coding tasks, 50% in deep research, 36% in scientific tasks — because the LLM-tool loop is strictly serial. Core abstraction is the 'Pattern Tuple' (context, prediction, function, probability), which decouples control-flow prediction (which tool comes next, mined as discrete 'Strong Chains' and 'Refinement Loops' over tool-signature sequences) from data-flow prediction (a symbolic value-mapping function that derives tool arguments from prior tool outputs without invoking the LLM). Measured control-flow regularities: 55% of successful file_editor write/replace calls are immediately followed by a terminal pytest/python call ('Edit-Verify' pattern); 38% of grep calls are immediately followed by file_editor ('Locate-Examine' pattern); in DeepResearch tasks, 51% of tool calls follow a search-then-visit funnel. A risk-aware opportunistic scheduler runs speculative tool calls only on transient idle compute/memory/IO slack, throttled by a dynamic slack budget, and instantly preempts speculative work the moment real (authoritative) demand appears, so mispredictions never slow the critical path; a unified result cache lets authoritative requests join an already-running speculative execution. Evaluated against ORION (serverless DAG execution) and SpecFaaS (speculative serverless execution) baselines on VirtualLab, Qwen Deep Research, and gemini-cli agents using real Azure Functions arrival traces for realistic bursty load: PASTE cuts average end-to-end task completion time by up to 48.5% (p95/p99 tail latency down 48.6%/61.9%), average speedup of 1.25x/1.32x over ORION/SpecFaaS; cuts average tool execution latency by up to 55.2% (1.71x/1.83x speedup over ORION/SpecFaaS); reduces tool-wait time by 67% versus both baselines and increases measured LLM/tool overlap by >10x versus SpecFaaS. The next-tool predictor itself achieves only 27.8% top-1 accuracy but 43.9% top-3 recall and 93.8% overall hit rate (because the scheduler can speculate on multiple ranked candidates within a bounded resource budget, so exact top-1 accuracy matters less than ranked-candidate coverage). Safety/side-effect audit: of >20,000 speculative actions across all workloads, 602 were flagged as potentially side-effecting and blocked from committing; no task produced an output different from authoritative-only execution. Overhead: 0.02 core-seconds CPU / 2.6MB memory / 0.9MB network per second of latency saved; pattern-prediction + scheduling overhead is under 100ms.

data.title: Frontier AI Cybersecurity Observatory
Sonar AI Agent Discovers Vulnerabilities Hidden in Business Logic Workflows | DevOps.com | DevOps.com
data.summary: Short news piece (DevOps.com, Mike Vizard, Aug 27 2026) on Sonar's launch of the 'SonarQube Hunter Agent,' an AI agent that analyzes an entire codebase to find three flaw categories: broken access control, business-logic vulnerabilities, and authentication/session-management issues -- categories that deterministic scanning tools (good at injection, unsafe data flow, insecure patterns) cannot detect because they require understanding how the code is SUPPOSED to function (e.g., privilege escalation only becomes visible with intended-behavior context, per Sonar's Satinder Khasriya). The agent traces how code and data move through the system (replacing manual testing/pentest work for this flaw class), identifies the developer who introduced any flagged issue, and surfaces verified findings directly inside CI/CD via DevSecOps integrations. Frames urgency around shrinking time-to-exploitation: AI now lets attackers find/exploit vulnerabilities in hours, while teams historically allocated only a few hours/month to patches that might ship months later -- implying DevSecOps teams need near-real-time patch deployment, verified malware-free, going forward.

data.title: Promptfoo vs DeepEval: LLM Testing Framework Comparison (2026) | genai.qa
data.summary: genai.qa vendor comparison (updated Sept 2026) of Promptfoo (Node/CLI, YAML-configured, MIT) vs DeepEval (Python/pytest-native, Apache 2.0) for LLM evaluation, noting OpenAI's March 2026 acquisition of Promptfoo. Promptfoo: 50+ assertion types, 40+ auto-generating red-team plugins (prompt injection direct/indirect, jailbreak one-shot/multi-turn, PII exposure, BOLA, SQL injection via LLM, excessive agency, system-prompt leak), 30+ LLM providers, built-in web UI; best for red-teaming/adversarial testing and multi-model A/B comparison. DeepEval: 14+ purpose-built metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, hallucination, bias, toxicity, tool correctness, task completion), GEval custom rubric-to-judge metric, native pytest CI integration, built-in MMLU/TruthfulQA/HellaSwag/GSM8K benchmarks; best for Python-native CI quality gates. Gives concrete cost comparison: at 10,000 evals/day, Promptfoo red-team+rubric runs ~00/day vs DeepEval's 4-metric suite ~00/day (DeepEval's metrics are all LLM-judged vs Promptfoo's many non-judge assertions). Recommends the production pattern of running both — Promptfoo as PR-blocking red-team gate, DeepEval as PR-blocking metric gate — and warns both tools are only ~85-92% accurate versus human raters, so 5-10% of flagged cases should get human review. Flags pitfalls: running full red-team scans on every commit is expensive (schedule nightly instead), and DeepEval thresholds calibrated in dev often break in production due to domain-distribution shift.

data.title:
Build Long-running AI agents that pause, resume, and never lose context with ADK
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
data.summary: Google Developers Blog tutorial (May 2026, authors Shubham Saboo and Eric Dong) on building long-running agents with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK), using a multi-week HR 'New Hire Onboarding Coordinator Agent' as the worked example. Argues stateless chat-history-replay agents break over multi-day workflows in three specific ways: prompt context pollution (irrelevant chatter accumulates over hundreds of turns), token cost explosion (replaying full multi-week history on every inference call), and reasoning hallucinations over idle time (model invents or skips steps after a long dormancy gap). The fix is three architectural shifts: (1) durable, explicit state-machine schemas (named constants like START/WELCOME_SENT/DOCUMENTS_SIGNED/IT_PROVISIONED/HARDWARE_DELIVERED/COMPLETED) read from session state rather than inferred from chat history; (2) event-driven dormancy instead of active polling or blocked threads -- the agent 'sleeps' via container scale-to-zero (Cloud Run) with session state persisted to SQLite/Cloud SQL via ADK's DatabaseSessionService, and external webhooks (e.g. /webhooks/document_signed) call runner.run_async with a state_delta to atomically transition state and wake the agent exactly once an external event arrives; (3) multi-agent delegation of specialized sub-tasks (e.g. a dedicated it_agent for IT provisioning) to keep each agent's prompt and tool set narrow. The piece is directly relevant to 'auto-killing idle agents': it demonstrates the inverse/complementary pattern -- rather than killing an agent on a clean health check, it shows how to let an agent instance scale to zero (equivalent to self-terminating the running process) while state survives in durable storage, then be woken deterministically by an external signal rather than continuing to poll or hold a blocked thread. It also shows ADK 'golden evaluation' tests that simulate 48-hour idle delays and assert the agent correctly refuses to skip workflow steps when prompted to -- a safety-gate test pattern applicable to verifying quiet self-termination/resume logic does not silently corrupt or skip state. Production deployment target is Google's Agent Runtime (Vertex AI agent engine), which handles session persistence, auto-scaling including scale-to-zero during idle time, and Cloud Trace telemetry for pause/resume latency.

data.title: AI Pricing Models Compared: Seats, Tokens, Outcomes | Zuora
data.summary: Zuora guide taxonomizing six AI SaaS pricing models directly relevant to Pillar 6 (subscription vs API economics): Per Seat, Per Token, Per Activity, Per Output, Per Outcome, and Hybrid. Key cited case: Wall Street Journal (Oct 2023) reported GitHub Copilot averaged a $20/user/month loss against a $10/user/month subscription price because heavy users' inference cost exceeded the seat fee by 2-3x -- the canonical example of per-seat pricing as a 'margin trap' when usage scales with engagement. Per Activity examples: Salesforce Agentforce at $2/AI-handled conversation; Anthropic Claude API billed per call across model tiers. Per Outcome examples: Intercom Fin charges per resolved support ticket; Zendesk charges per autonomous resolution -- this model transfers cost-variance risk from buyer to seller and requires tight unit economics. Hybrid (subscription base + consumption overage or prepaid credits) is described as the dominant pattern for mature production AI businesses, citing Microsoft Security Copilot's Security Compute Unit (SCU) hourly-rate-plus-overage model and Adobe Firefly's prepaid credit-pack model. Introduces the COMPASS Framework (Scope of Work: Task/Process/Goal crossed with Level of Attribution: Diffuse/Medium/Direct) for choosing a pricing model, and names three common pitfalls: cost-plus thinking, pricing complexity creep (too many simultaneous meters), and soft-ROI positioning.

data.title: How Are AI Agents Used in Penetration Testing? | Synack
data.summary: Synack learning-center guide on agentic AI in penetration testing, centered on their production system 'Sara,' an agentic AI that plans/executes testing tasks, generates hypotheses, and collects evidence alongside the Synack Red Team while humans validate exploitability and impact. Key framework: agents suit structured/repeatable tasks (reconnaissance, enumeration, hypothesis generation, evidence drafting) while humans remain the checkpoint for exploitability, business impact, and high-risk decisions -- given in a table mapping each testing activity to where agents help vs. where human validation stays essential. Describes two multi-agent topologies: horizontal/parallel (specialized agents side-by-side under central orchestration, for broad simultaneous coverage) and vertical/hierarchical (routine collection at lower levels, escalation/consequential reasoning at higher levels, for controlled accountability). Governance prescription: define and document agent-authorized scope, require human sign-off on high-risk/irreversible actions, log all agent decisions/tool use for audit, periodically re-check agent output against human-validated findings to catch drift. Cites OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as reference governance structures. States agents 'cannot fully replace' human pentesters and lists failure modes: false positives from misjudged context, operational risk from unenforced guardrails, hard-to-interpret decisions absent audit logging, and attack paths requiring human creativity.

data.title: AI Code Quality Gates: An Automated Review Pipeline | Axiom Studio
data.summary: Axiom Studio (VibeFlow) vendor blog proposing a four-gate CI pipeline for AI-agent-generated commits, citing Perry et al. 2023 (Stanford) finding developers using AI assistants wrote less secure code while rating it as more secure, and GitClear commit analysis showing downward pressure on code quality with Copilot adoption. Gate 1 (style/correctness): formatter + linter with zero-tolerance for suppressions (ESLint/Ruff/golangci-lint) + strict-mode type checker + clean build. Gate 2 (security): Semgrep/CodeQL taint analysis, OSV-Scanner dependency scanning, Gitleaks/TruffleHog secret detection, plus prompt/config injection scanning referencing OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Gate 3 (test coverage): diff-level coverage threshold (diff-cover), mutation testing (pitest/Stryker/mutmut) to verify tests would actually catch a regression, and property-based tests (Hypothesis/fast-check). Gate 4 (compliance): framework tagging to SOC 2 CC6 / NIST AI RMF Measure, audit-trail capture (prompt, agent identity, model version, human approver), and policy-as-code (OPA/Conftest/Cedar) checks. Recommends parallelizing slow gates after a fast lint pass and risk-tiering gate intensity by code blast radius.

data.title: Pricing models explained: Per-seat vs. flat-rate AI notetakers for sales | Granola
data.summary: Granola (vendor) blog on AI notetaker pricing models (per-seat vs. flat-rate), tangential to the software-factory brief but useful as a general SaaS-AI pricing comparison for Pillar 6. Documents concrete pricing data points: Granola Business $14/user/mo, Enterprise $35/user/mo; Otter.ai Pro $8.33/user/mo capped at 1,200 transcription min/mo with 90-min/conversation limit; Fireflies.ai Pro $10/seat/mo capped at 8,000 storage min/seat; Gong ~$250/user/mo plus mandatory $5K-$50K/year platform fee plus $7,500 onboarding; Chorus/ZoomInfo ~$100-200/user/mo plus base fee. Provides a TCO formula: Annual license cost + implementation cost + annual admin cost without tool - annual admin cost with tool. Cites HubSpot data that 32% of sales reps spend 1+ hour/day on CRM data entry, and industry data that 43% of sales professionals spend 10-20 hrs/week on note-taking/CRM entry. Illustrates the general SaaS principle (echoed in the Zuora note) that flat per-seat pricing breaks down when usage caps or platform fees hide true cost, relevant by analogy to agent subscription-vs-API tradeoffs.

data.title: How to Understand a Legacy Codebase Using AI Before Changing it
data.summary: Dense (3,915-word) practitioner tutorial (freeCodeCamp, Hugo Teijiz) prescribing a 10-step 'codebase archaeology' workflow to run BEFORE any AI-assisted refactor/migration, built around the discipline 'do not propose a refactor yet.' Steps: map the repository (treat directory names as evidence, not truth), choose one concrete business capability, trace it end-to-end through entry point -> business logic -> state change -> external call -> output, separate business rules from infrastructure (classify each line as business-rule/orchestration/persistence/caching/messaging/unknown), find hidden side effects (log synchronicity, retryability, idempotency -- warns a crash between chargeCard() and markOrderAsPaid() can double-charge on retry), discover implicit contracts (API/event/DB schemas consumed outside the module), find duplicated business rules without assuming they must be merged, build a lightweight module dependency map restricted to evidence from imports/constructor-deps/explicit calls, and explicitly record an 'Open Questions' list of what cannot be answered from the repo alone. Prescribes a validation hierarchy for AI claims: repository search (ripgrep), tests, DB schema, logs/telemetry, and git history (git log -S, git blame) -- 'AI should accelerate search, not replace it.' Explicitly warns against premature high-level prompts ('Rewrite using Clean Architecture', 'Convert to microservices') because they presuppose a solution before establishing what the system needs. Core thesis: 'changing code you understand is engineering; changing code you don't understand is experimentation,' and uncertainty ('I cannot determine why this condition exists') is treated as valuable AI output, not failure. LONG SOURCE — candidate for source-analyst deep dive given density of reusable prompts.

data.title: Claude API Pricing: A Complete Guide for AI Teams in 2026 | Coworker AI
data.summary: Coworker.ai (vendor, promotes its own routing product) breakdown of Claude API token economics for 2026. Four tiers: Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 per MTok in/out; Sonnet 5 $2/$10 through Aug 31 2026 then $3/$15; Opus 4.8 $5/$25; Fable 5 $10/$50 -- a 5x input/output multiplier spanning the stack. Output tokens cost 5x input across all tiers. Prompt caching: cache hits cost 10% of standard input price (e.g. Sonnet cached reads $0.30/MTok vs $3.00 standard, Haiku $0.10 vs $1.00); cites a real deployment (Sonnet 4.6 restaurant ordering system, 7 locations) achieving 97% cache-hit rate. Batch API gives flat 50% discount on input+output across all tiers (Opus drops to $2.50/$12.50) with up to 24h latency; a 100K-doc/day extraction workload reportedly saves ~$219K/year switching to batch. Cites Anthropic Economic Index Sept 2025 Report: agentic/multi-turn tasks are >50% of enterprise API token consumption, and resending full conversation history means a 14-token question costs fractions of a cent early in a session but >$2 by the 260th exchange; trimming to last 5-10 turns + summarizing older turns cut bills 40-60% for 10K-conversation/month workloads. Notes Sonnet 5+ use a newer tokenizer generating ~30% more tokens for the same text. Cites a Coworker LinkedIn post claiming a company's Claude spend grew from $500K/month to $10M as volume scaled without updated routing logic -- illustrative of unconstrained agentic cost blowup, directly relevant to Pillar 6 cost optimization.

data.title: Automated Penetration Testing | AI Pentest Agent | Simbian
data.summary: Vendor marketing page for Simbian's AI Pentest Agent (claims deployment across 300+ enterprise environments). Marketing claims should be treated as low-confidence/unverified: the page's headline stat counters (Remediation Time Reduction %, False Positive Reduction %, Retests Included) rendered as '0' in the fetched static HTML, meaning the actual percentage figures are JS-animated and were not captured — a notable absence worth flagging rather than citing as hard numbers. Architecture relevant to Pillar 3 (automated security sweeps): a 'Context Lake' enriches every automated pentest with org-specific priorities, past findings, and asset criticality so scope/prioritization isn't generic CVSS-only; adaptive probe generation claims no pre-scripted playbooks, instead generating test cases dynamically based on live application response; covers OWASP Top 10 'and beyond' with standard automated pentests described as running 6+ hours; includes safe-mode kill switches and sandboxed exploitation to avoid production disruption; and provides full 'AI reasoning traces' — an explicit audit log of why a given attack vector was chosen, framed as an anti-black-box transparency mechanism (directly relevant to adversarial model review / why-this-decision logging for the Zero-Hallucination pillar). Workflow stages described: Learn & Plan -> Scan & Enumeration -> Assess Vulnerability -> Exploit & Validate -> Report -> Remediate & Retest, explicitly feeding findings back into separate SOC Agent and Threat Hunt Agent products (a named multi-agent, closed-loop security-ops architecture: PenTest/SOC/Threat-Hunt/SecDevOps agents operating as specialized departments). FAQ section explicitly states human pentesters remain necessary for 'complex business logic, social engineering, physical security, and strategic risk advisory' and cites a hybrid human-AI certification partnership (LRQA) — a vendor acknowledgment that full automation of pentesting is not yet complete. Customer testimonials (Matillion, Axelar, Cybalt, SMT, Wipro, Bottomline) are promotional and should not be treated as independent verification.

data.title: Idle shutdown  |  Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform  |  Google Cloud Documentation
data.summary: Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Workbench documentation on infra-level idle shutdown: Workbench instances (notebook/agent execution VMs) auto-shut-down after a configurable period of inactivity (default 180 minutes, range 10-1440 min in console, any integer seconds via idle-timeout-seconds metadata key or Terraform). Activity is defined narrowly as kernel activity on 127.0.0.1:8080/api/{sessions,terminals,kernels} -- CPU usage alone does NOT reset the timer, so a compute-bound but interaction-idle instance will still be killed. Billing stops for CPU/GPU while shut down (disk storage charges persist). Scheduled executions still run on schedule even while the instance is in a shut-down state, implying the platform treats 'shut down' as a dormant/resumable state rather than destroyed. This is infra-level (VM lifecycle) auto-termination rather than an agent-logic self-termination decision, but it is the mechanism a software-factory architecture would layer agent-level 'quiet self-terminate on clean health check' logic on top of.

data.title: Context Engineering | Compaction & Agent Memory for Automated Malware Analysis | SentinelOne
data.summary: SentinelLABS (Gabriel Bernadett-Shapiro, updated Jul 2026) benchmark of OpenAI's native Responses API compaction feature on an automated malware-analysis agent evaluation harness (decompiler access; scored against golden reference reports). Measured results across long-running agent evals: input tokens -86%, output tokens -31%, reasoning tokens -33%, one fewer model call per run, and aggregate evaluation score 'effectively unchanged' -- except domain-object-modeling score (recovering higher-level malware object/type structures) measurably decreased, flagged as analytically significant since object/type recovery is often the most valuable conclusion in malware analysis. Core architectural principle: separate compacted 'working memory' (current goal, hypotheses, what's been tried) from durable external storage (decompiled functions, tool logs, ground-truth artifacts) -- compaction should never be relied on to preserve exact evidence verbatim. Documents two OpenAI compaction modes with code: server-side (context_management threshold in responses.create, automatic) vs. standalone (/responses/compact endpoint, explicit control at phase boundaries) with a decision table for when to use each. Six practical rules given: separate working memory from source-of-truth; compact only long-running workflows; start with server-side; never evaluate cost alone; preserve negative/failed-path information; treat compaction as lossy until proven otherwise via evals/traces. Frames context engineering (what gets compressed/retrieved/discarded across turns) as potentially as important as model selection for long-horizon agents. Cites Anthropic 'Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents,' LangChain Deep Agents context-engineering docs, and arXiv:2601.07190 on context compression for long-horizon agents.

data.title: Artificial Intelligence Security Issues: Coding Agent Risks | Fiddler AI Blog
data.summary: Fiddler AI vendor blog arguing autonomous coding agents break traditional human-in-the-loop security assumptions since the agent is both author and reviewer. Identifies five agent-specific risk categories traditional tools miss: (1) credential/secret exposure in generated code/commits (cites GitGuardian State of Secrets Sprawl 2024); (2) prompt injection through code context -- malicious instructions embedded in comments, READMEs, issue descriptions (cites Simon Willison 2022, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps, and arXiv:2601.17548 on agentic coding assistant prompt injection); (3) unauthorized tool invocations absent scoped allowlists (cites NIST AI RMF 1.0); (4) unauditable decision chains -- no commit-message-equivalent record of agent reasoning; (5) shadow agent proliferation -- informal agent deployments with personal access tokens (cites OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026). Recommends treating coding agents as non-human IAM identities with scoped/rotatable credentials, pre-LLM and post-execution guardrails (secret/PII redaction, prompt-injection blocking), span-level tracing of every tool call/LLM call/sub-agent decision, and a governance checklist (inventory agents, assign NHIs, allowlist tools, instrument telemetry, deploy guardrails, monitor behavioral anomalies, maintain auditable traces). Cites a directional estimate of ~$260K/year at 500K traces/day for external evaluation API costs as the 'AI Trust Tax' Fiddler's in-environment Trust Models avoid.

data.title: Understanding Security Risks of AI Agents’ Dependency Updates
data.summary: Purdue University arXiv paper (2601.00205, Jan 2026, Singla, Cakar, Amusuo, Davis), large-scale empirical study of 117,062 dependency changes across 33,596 agent-authored PRs (Copilot, Devin, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Claude Code) and 6,618 human-authored PRs across 2,807 GitHub repos (over 100 stars) and seven package ecosystems, using the AIDev-pop dataset plus the ecosyste.ms vulnerability database (aggregating GitHub Security Advisories and OSV) for PR-time-known vulnerability labeling. Core finding directly quantifies agent code-change risk and blast radius for a software-factory quality-control design: agents select PR-time known-vulnerable dependency versions more often than humans (2.46 percent vs 1.64 percent of additions and updates), and when agents do introduce a vulnerable version, remediation is harder, 36.8 percent of agent cases require a major-version upgrade to reach a patched release vs only 12.9 percent for human cases, despite patched alternatives existing in most cases. At the fleet level this nets out to agent-authored dependency work producing a net vulnerability increase of 98 across the sample, while human-authored dependency work produces a net vulnerability reduction of 1,316 over the same period. Agents also update dependency versions more frequently than humans conditional on touching a manifest (25.5 percent vs 15.8 percent) but spread edits across many small PRs rather than bundling them like humans do. The authors explicitly recommend PR-time vulnerability screening and registry-aware guardrails as mitigations, a direct measured justification for the blast radius and adversarial review pillars of an autonomous software-factory architecture.

data.title: What is AI Agent Orchestration? Guide to Multi-Agent Systems | Wiz
data.summary: Wiz (cloud security vendor) academy guide on AI agent orchestration security -- strong source for the whitepaper's zero-hallucination/quality-control and Director/Worker infrastructure pillars, framed from the attack-surface angle. Defines orchestration lifecycle (task decomposition, agent selection/delegation, execution/data flow, state management, result assembly/feedback) and distinguishes it from deterministic workflow tools (Airflow, Step Functions) by its runtime, non-deterministic routing based on intermediate results. Catalogs five orchestration patterns with security implications: sequential, concurrent, hierarchical (top orchestrator delegating to mid-level orchestrators managing their own sub-agents -- i.e., Director/Worker), event-driven (decoupled pub/sub, harder to trace/debug), and federated (cross-org orchestrator coordination with trust/governance challenges). Core security claims: prompt injection into an orchestrator achieves 'up to 71% attack success rates' in research settings when manipulating agent tool-selection decisions; multi-agent systems create a 'trust cascade' where compromising one node poisons downstream agent context/actions; of over 12,000 tools across 1,360 MCP servers surveyed, researchers found 43% of publicly available MCP server implementations contained command injection flaws and 30% permitted unrestricted URL fetching. Cites Wiz's State of AI in the Cloud 2025 report finding 85% of organizations now use AI services/tools. Recommends concrete mitigations directly applicable to the 'blast radius' pillar: per-agent scoped IAM identities (separate read-only vs. write/action roles) rather than shared broad permissions, tool allowlists per agent, secrets brokering with short-lived credentials over static API keys, egress controls restricting outbound domains, and structured audit logs with correlation IDs across agent/tool invocations. Lists common production pitfalls: treating orchestration as deterministic (testing only happy-path misses emergent runtime behavior), granting agents developer-equivalent permissions, no agent-to-agent observability, ignoring blast radius of shared memory/context stores, and no enforced tool allowlist turning orchestration into an 'unbounded execution plane.'

data.title: Vulnerability Blast Radius: How to Measure and Reduce Impact | Blog | Endor Labs
data.summary: Endor Labs (AppSec vendor) blog defining vulnerability blast radius as the scope of systems, data, and users a flaw can reach once exploited, covering both the specific BlastRADIUS protocol CVE (CVE-2024-3596, a 30-year-old MD5-collision forgery flaw in RADIUS authentication disclosed July 2024, CVSS 9.0 plus) and the general blast-radius-as-prioritization concept for vulnerability management. States CVE submissions are up 263 percent since 2020, making blast-radius-based triage necessary since most scanners only report that a CVE exists, not whether it is reachable. Defines measurement methodology: static call-graph analysis plus dependency mapping (direct and transitive) to determine reachability, noting full-stack reachability analysis typically reduces actionable findings by 90 percent or more versus raw CVE counts; a CVE in an imported-but-never-called library has zero blast radius in practice. Cites Black Ducks OSSRA finding that transitive dependencies make up 64 percent of open-source components in typical applications (often invisible in manifest files), and the Log4Shell case (CVE-2021-44228) where vulnerable Log4j versions still represented 13 percent of downloads years post-disclosure due to deep transitive chains. Identifies four blast-radius amplifiers directly relevant to agent-driven code change risk: deep transitive dependency chains, shared libraries and common base images (concentration risk), privileged-access and credential-exposure vulnerabilities, and flat, unsegmented network architecture.

data.title: AI Agent Evaluation: Metrics, Traces, Human Review, and Workflows - Confident AI
data.summary: Confident AI / DeepEval engineering guide (7,480 words, dense -- candidate for source-analyst deep-dive) on agent evaluation architecture, directly load-bearing for pillars 1 (rigid evals) and 5 (continuous operation). Core taxonomy: single-turn vs multi-turn agents distinguished strictly by count of end-to-end user interactions (not internal agent-to-agent handoffs, which are 'component-level interactions'). Agents fail at two levels: end-to-end (task not completed, infinite reasoning/retry loops, unacceptable cost/latency/friction) and component-level (wrong tool args, tool outputs misused, bad handoffs, tool-call hallucination, circular/echoing spans with no new work). Four named failure patterns with concrete scenarios: 'the ghost action' (agent claims a booking/API call happened when it never did -- false task completion that scores highly on output-only metrics because the final text is fluent); 'the interrogation loop' (agent re-asks for info the user already gave because parameter extraction silently fails); 'the confident fabricator' (stale/fabricated data flows into a polished-looking report because intermediate tool outputs were never validated -- a component-level failure cascading to end-to-end); 'the budget burner' (task completion passes but the agent issues 14 LLM completions per ticket via redundant re-querying/re-explaining, and cost 10x's without latency/budget monitoring catching it). Prescribes three-step eval pipeline: (1) trace every component/interaction via LLM tracing/OpenTelemetry-style spans, (2) attach metrics (DeepEval's @observe decorator) at the correct span level, (3) construct test cases/goldens. Names concrete agentic metrics with defined mechanics: Task Completion (single-turn end-to-end, infers intended goal from trace then verifies against final output), Argument Correctness (component-level, scores whether tool-call parameters are correct/relevant), Tool Correctness (reference-based exact-match against expected tool list, run offline not online), Conversation Completeness and Turn Relevancy (multi-turn, sliding-window judged against full turn history), Handoff Correctness, Turn Faithfulness. For conversational agents specifically recommends layering Conversation Relevancy, Knowledge Retention, and Role Adherence metrics. Advocates 'operating envelopes' as explicit CI gates distinct from LLM-judge scores: max steps, max tool calls, token budget, wall-clock timeout per golden/scenario -- quality-passes-but-economics-fails is treated as a hard CI failure. Lays out a 'Swiss cheese' layered-defense model: automated evals (fast, reproducible, but blind to unmodeled real traffic) + production monitoring/traces (catches real edge cases but reactive) + sampled human review with a versioned rubric (calibrates judges, catches 'metric green, user red' cases, explicitly NOT exhaustive) + user feedback (sparse but grounded) -- no single layer is sufficient alone. Recommends a four-stage ship workflow: local/CI gate on goldens+envelopes, pre-release human sampling of a fixed trace set after any prompt/tool/model change, production monitoring with periodic audits of flagged sessions, and closing the loop by converting every disagreement/incident into a new golden so the same failure can't recur silently.

data.title: Automata from Agent Traces:
data.summary: ArXiv paper (Cho et al., Holistic AI / UCL, ICML 2026 AIWILD workshop) proposing a method to extract a compact deterministic finite-state machine (FSM) from a corpus of LLM-agent execution traces using only positive examples, then using that FSM as a unified substrate for workflow memory, next-step (skill) prediction, failure prediction, and runtime monitoring. Method: traces are tokenized into an 'activity alphabet' (tool-call names, action tags, or command categories, 6-42 symbols), inserted into a prefix tree, then merged via a 'last-activity right congruence' (states sharing the same incoming activity are merged), producing |A|+1 states deterministically with no hyperparameters, in 1-110ms. Across 12 public agent-trace datasets (SWE-agent, WebArena, AgentNet, tau2-bench airline/retail/telecom, ATBench, OSWorld, SWE-smith, etc.), the resulting FSMs have only 7-43 states yet replay held-out traces at >=0.997 fitness, versus RPNI needing 382-63,897 states (15-3,036x more) for comparable fitness, and versus Alergia needing 1.0-6.0x more states. For next-step/skill prediction, conditioning on current FSM state (an order-1 Markov predictor over the learned automaton) cuts cross-entropy by 62% versus a unigram baseline and by 21% (0.155 bits) versus raw-context baselines without FSM state; a minimal natural-language prompt format (next-action probabilities + top-15 multi-step continuations from the current state) beats Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) on LLM-judged top-1 next-action accuracy on all 8 tested datasets, with gains from +0.8pp (tau2-bench airline) to +25.3pp (SWE-smith). For failure prediction, per-state behavioral + cross-entropy anomaly features feed a single gradient-boosted classifier reaching held-out AUROC up to 0.941 (tau2-bench telecom), and lift MLP/GRU/Transformer sequence baselines on 20 of 21 dataset-architecture pairs. A lightweight online monitor (cycle-rate > 0.778 threshold plus minimum unique-state count) achieves rank-AUROC 0.66 at the 25% trace-completion checkpoint and triggers early stopping at 32% completion on SWE-agent (precision 85.9%, recall 95.5%, saving 68% of remaining compute). The paper also finds FSM topology is largely model-invariant: a single FSM built across 4 different LLMs on tau2-bench achieves 1.000 fitness on each model individually, sharing an 80-92% dominant transition backbone, which the authors interpret as behavioral structure being shaped more by the deployment harness/tool-set than by the underlying LLM. Limitations acknowledged: the FSM captures the directly-follows closure of observed traces (not the true generating language, per Gold's 1967 theorem), activity-extraction function is dataset-specific, and broader cross-architecture/cross-domain transfer is untested.

data.title: The Cron Layer: How I Taught My AI Agent to Work Autonomously 24/7 - DEV Community
data.summary: Named-practitioner (Ryan Wynar, byldr.co, South Florida) Dev.to post (gray-literature, low authority but directly on-topic) describing a working 'cron layer' for continuous autonomous agent operation -- concrete, documented production architecture for the whitepaper's triggers/continuous-operation pillar. Architecture: a gateway daemon called 'OpenClaw' manages scheduled cron jobs, each with three parts -- Schedule (cron expression/interval/one-shot), Payload (prompt injected as a system event or full agent turn), and Session target (shared main session vs. isolated standalone session). Documents a real daily schedule: 5 prospect-finding runs at 10am/1pm/3pm/5pm/8pm across 4 sales campaigns (deduping against a PostgreSQL queue), an 8am LinkedIn draft job, a 7pm auto-blog job cross-posting to Dev.to/Hashnode, and a 30-minute heartbeat job. Reports a concrete failure mode from running everything in one shared session early on: the prospect-finder agent would burn context with 200+ lead records, causing the subsequent blog-writer job to hallucinate (e.g., inventing dentists in Fort Lauderdale) -- fixed by giving every cron job its own fresh, isolated session that reports back and discards state. States that deduplication logic (checking phone numbers and business names against the existing queue) is the 'most underrated part' of automated prospecting, reporting 40-60% duplicate rates on any given search against a 237-prospect queue. Self-reported 10-day results: 100+ new qualified prospects added, 50+ automated search sessions run, multiple blog posts published with no manual keyboard input.

data.title: AI Code Review Only Catches Half of Your Bugs – O’Reilly
data.summary: O'Reilly Radar article (Andrew Stellman, Apr 2026, part 5 of an agentic-engineering series) argues AI code review hits an 'intent ceiling': structural analysis (linters, SAST, AI reviewers) can only catch bugs visible from code alone, but roughly half of security defects are design flaws/intent violations invisible without a specification of what the code is SUPPOSED to do. Cites NIST SATE evaluations finding best static analysis tools plateau at 50-60% detection for security vulnerabilities; Gary McGraw's 'Software Security: Building Security In' (2006) splitting defects ~50/50 implementation bugs vs design flaws; Charoenwet et al. (ISSTA 2024) testing 5 SAST tools against 815 real vulnerability-contributing commits, finding 22% of vulnerable commits entirely undetected and 76% of warnings in vulnerable functions irrelevant; CWE-862 Missing Authorization ranked #9 on the 2024 CWE Top 25. Proposes deriving 'negative requirements' from chat logs, GitHub issues, and design discussions to give AI reviewers intent to check against — exemplified by a confirmed/merged fix to Google's Gson library (PR #3006) found by analyzing GitHub issues #676/#913/#948/#1558. Describes a four-step method: AI lists observed behavioral contracts, derives requirements, checks coverage, asserts completeness and loops back on gaps. Discloses the author's own patent application tied to the open-source 'Quality Playbook' tool.

data.title: Top 5 LLM Evaluation Frameworks in 2026, Compared | DeepEval - The LLM Evaluation Framework
data.summary: DeepEvals (vendor, but structured feature-comparison) 2026 comparison of five LLM evaluation frameworks, DeepEval, Promptfoo, Ragas, Arize Phoenix, TruLens, scored across 8 criteria: metric coverage, dataset management, AI-agent tracing (tracing a failed score back to the specific tool, retriever, LLM-call, or sub-agent that caused it), developer workflow integration (local, CI/CD, usable by coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex as an evaluation harness), synthetic dataset generation, multi-turn conversation simulation, ecosystem integrations, and path-to-production (shared reports, regression analysis, online monitoring). Defines the category boundary precisely: an evaluation framework differs from an academic benchmark (fixed task comparison, e.g. MMLU), an evaluation platform (managed team layer), an observability platform (production traces, latency, cost), and a guardrail (live request interception), useful terminology for distinguishing eval tooling from monitoring tooling in an agentic pipeline. Rated DeepEval and Arize Phoenix Strong on AI-agent tracing and multi-agent metric coverage; Promptfoo rated Strong on prompt testing and AI security but explicitly Not supported on native component-level agent tracing; Ragas rated Partial, RAG-first coverage with only some agent metrics.

data.title: CrewAI vs LangGraph vs AutoGen: Choosing the Right Multi-Agent AI Framework | DataCamp
data.summary: DataCamp tutorial comparing CrewAI, LangGraph, and AutoGen multi-agent frameworks across architecture, memory, human-in-the-loop, caching/replay, code execution, scalability, and enterprise readiness.
